title: How Superradiance Survives Molecular Noise inside Virus Capsids
authors: Tianran Li, Irina Tsvetkova, Matthew Brauser, Amala Raj, Philip Shushkov, Bogdan Dragnea
abstract: Excited organic dyes chemically bound to an icosahedral virus shell can spontaneously synchronize and emit a superradiant burst of light. The mechanism that allows it to occur at room temperature, despite collisional dephasing and inhomogeneous broadening, is not understood. Few other known low-dimensional condensed matter systems exhibit room-temperature superradiance (SR). In the fluctuation-prone environment of molecular-based systems, electron--vibrational coupling has been proposed to play a central role. Here, we addressed experimentally the existence of underdamped virus capsid phonon-like modes and theoretically their involvement in the transition from uncorrelated to cooperative emission. We find that SR-active dye-labeled capsids exhibit underdamped low-frequency oscillations that modulate the dye excited-state response, and modeling shows how such capsid motion can promote the collective polarization required for superradiant emission.
summary: This research investigates how superradiance can persist at room temperature in dye-labeled virus capsids, a process normally hindered by molecular noise. The authors propose that coherent, underdamped capsid vibrations act as a dynamic structural element, coupling to the dye excitons to restore the necessary collective polarization for light emission. By combining TA spectroscopy and theoretical modeling, they provide evidence for this phonon-mediated mechanism.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental mechanism enabling superradiance (SR) to occur at room temperature despite significant molecular noise sources like collisional dephasing.
main_result: The authors find that underdamped, low-frequency collective vibrations (phonons) of the virus capsid are necessary to dynamically modulate the exciton-exciton interaction, thereby promoting the collective polarization required for SR.
method: The study combines ultrafast spectroscopy (Transient Absorption) experiments on dye-labeled virus capsids with theoretical modeling of coupled quantum oscillators.
model_or_system: The system involves excited organic dyes chemically bound to an icosahedral virus shell (BOGs). The model treats the dye excitation as coupled to the collective, low-frequency vibrational modes of the capsid, which act as a dynamic environment.
key_observables: Superradiant emission intensity, oscillatory modulation in TA residuals, and the detection of low-frequency vibrational peaks ($\approx 1.3 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$).
important_parameters: Room temperature, underdamped frequency ($\approx 1 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$), and the coupling strength between the dye excitons and the capsid motion.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed low-frequency modes are acoustic-like, underdamped phonons, and that SR recovery requires modulation of the exciton-exciton interaction, not just individual site energies.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the SR emission profile. Figure 2 shows oscillatory modulation in TA residuals for BOGs. Figure 3 shows the detection of a low-frequency peak ($\approx 1.3 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$) in AuVLP TA traces. Figure 4 simulates that SR only reappears when the vibration modulates the exciton-exciton interaction.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (SR at room temperature), presents experimental evidence for low-frequency oscillations in BOGs and AuVLPs, and concludes with theoretical modeling demonstrating that these coherent vibrations are the active ingredient promoting the necessary collective polarization for SR.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it models quantum coherence (SR) in a complex, open, and noisy solid-state/biological environment, using vibrational modes as the mediating coupling mechanism, which is a core topic in cavity QED and molecular physics.
